name: Isaiah 'Church' Bell
languages: Italian (a soldier's Italian, learned in Tuscany)
equipment: Leather jacket, brown, cut big across the shoulders, over a white shirt his mother irons
.45 automatic (Colt M1911, Army issue, which he was supposed to hand back), 7 rounds loaded
Brass knuckles, which he dislikes and carries anyway
Hand wraps and a mouthguard in his jacket pocket, from habit
A pocket Bible with his mother's name in the front and a pressed flower from Italy in Psalms
A first-aid kit, small, for cuts over the eye
His Local 9 card, paid up, and his boxing licence, lapsed
A thermos of coffee and two ham sandwiches wrapped in wax paper
features: Seen Worse (Ex-Service origin: advantage on saves against being frightened and against the Shaken condition; the first time each combat he is hit by a firearm, he keeps his reaction and any readied action)

Hard Knocks (Heavy: unarmed strikes deal 1d6 + STR; once per turn an extra 1d4 bludgeoning with an unarmed strike or a bludgeoning Melee weapon such as brass knuckles; anyone he drops with one is knocked out unless he chooses otherwise, and he can deliver a knockout blow with his fists)
Thick Skull (Heavy: advantage on CON saves against knockout blows and being stunned; once per long rest, when reduced to 0 hit points but not killed outright, he drops to 1 instead)

The Look (Heavy, 2nd level: as an action, one creature within 30 ft that can see him makes a WIS save, DC 13, or is frightened of him until the end of his next turn; outside combat, a failed save means it answers one question truthfully)
Style: Bruiser (Heavy, 3rd level: his unarmed strikes deal 1d8 + STR, and when he takes the Attack action he can make one unarmed strike or grapple as a bonus action)

Fight Crowd (Prizefighter background: in every gym, boxing club and waterfront bar in Port Calloway someone remembers 'Church' Bell, middleweight, 1946 to 1949, twenty-two wins and three losses; he can always find a sparring partner, a cut man, a bed, and a man who will tell him the truth about a fixed fight)

personality.traits: I am big and quiet and I let people underestimate me. I say grace before every meal, out loud, even in a diner, even when it embarrasses people. I hate bullies with a cold, patient hatred, and I have never once hit a man who was not trying to hit someone else.
personality.ideals: A strong man has a duty to the weak. That is the whole of it. My mother says it is the whole of the Gospel too, and I am not going to argue with my mother.
personality.bonds: Danny Kessling got me my Local 9 card in 1941, when the union did not want men like me, and stood up in the hall and said that if Bell could not have a card then neither could he. I was nineteen. I went to his execution vigil in 1947 and stood in the rain all night and I have never believed he did it.
personality.flaws: When I get angry I go very calm, and then I hurt somebody, and I am ashamed of how good it feels. I fight a man in the ring for money. Outside it, I am never sure I will be able to stop.

appearance: A tall, powerful Black man of thirty with a boxer's broad flat face, a scar through his left eyebrow from a fight he won and another along his jaw from one in Italy, close-cut hair and very gentle brown eyes. He dresses neatly and plainly. He is unnervingly light on his feet for his size and sits very still.
backstory: Isaiah Bell came up from Louisiana with his mother in 1940 to work in the Port Calloway canneries, and at nineteen got a Local 9 card because Danny Kessling made the union give him one. In 1943 he was drafted into the 92nd Infantry Division, a Black division with white officers, and fought up the west coast of Italy through the Gothic Line, which he does not talk about. He came home with a Bronze Star and a fighter's record from the Army boxing team and fought professionally out of the Calloway Athletic Club as a middleweight until 1949, when a promoter told him to lose a fight to a white boy from Spokane and he refused, and won, and could not get another bout in the state. He worked the docks, and then Walt Embry hired him after watching him stop three men from beating a drunk outside a bar on Front Street without throwing a punch. They call him Church because of the grace, and because he sings bass in the choir at Mount Zion on Sundays, and because, when he does finally hit someone, it is like the wrath of God. When the DA hires the agency to find out who wants him dead, Isaiah finds out on Tuesday morning that the case is about Danny Kessling, and he goes very calm.
